title: Stocking Drywall
short_answer: Board goes in the room where it gets hung, stacked in hang order — flat, off the slab, out of the weather, with specialty types separated and labeled.
summary: Board is heavy, fragile, awkward, and moisture-sensitive all at once. Nothing else we handle punishes a bad plan this hard — in damaged material and in backs.
plain_words: Board goes in the room where it gets hung, stacked in the order it gets hung. Flat, off the floor, out of the weather. On a good job the hanger's first move of the day is picking up a sheet, not looking for one.
when_to_use: Drywall delivery day — before the driver leaves
Staging board to rooms before hang mobilizes
Any time specialty board (MR, abuse-resistant, rated, shaftwall) must be separated from standard stock
prerequisites: Room-by-room quantities from the takeoff — not one pile per floor
Delivery method arranged (boom truck, telehandler, or window stocking — not stairs as the plan)
GC confirmation of allowable floor loading on suspended slabs before staging
Weather-tight storage area or cover plan if board cannot get wet

materials.name: Gypsum board per takeoff (standard and specialty types separated)
Working overage per room (avoid end-of-job sheet hunts)

steps.body: Flat, not on edge, for anything but short-term staging. Board stored on edge bows, and a bowed sheet fights you all day.
Off the slab on sleepers or dunnage — concrete wicks moisture into the bottom sheets.
On a flat, level base. A stack on uneven ground bows every sheet in it.
If it must lean, lean it close to vertical against something solid.
Away from unsealed exterior walls, open windows, and anywhere water can find it.
Stacked in the order it gets used, with the first sheets on top.
Out of the middle of the room where it blocks layout and ceiling work.
Count matches the ticket; ticket matches the order.
Damaged sheets pulled out and noted — not buried mid-stack for a hanger to find.
Nothing blocking egress, panels, or another trade.
Stacks stable, flat, off the slab, out of the weather.
Photos taken, ticket to the office.

warnings.title: Floor loading — ask, don't assume
warnings.body: A stack of board is one of the heaviest concentrated loads that will ever sit on a suspended floor. Confirm the allowable load with the GC before staging, and spread stacks out rather than piling one large stack in a single spot. Keep stacks away from the middle of long unsupported spans. If nobody can tell you the number, that's your answer — split the load.

warnings.title: Injury — the real cost center
warnings.body: Board handling is where our people get hurt: backs, hands, and crush injuries when a stack shifts. Use panel carts and panel carriers, two-person lifts on full sheets, gloves, and a stable stack that can't tip. A single lost-time back injury costs more than the equipment for a whole year — and costs the person a great deal more than that.

variations.title: Boom truck / crane delivery
variations.when: Above grade or multi-story — default when possible
changes: Places board directly on the working floor or through a window opening
Safer than people carrying board up stairs

variations.title: Window stocking
changes: Coordinate well in advance — the window open today may be glazed next week
Telehandler or forklift where site and openings allow

variations.title: Hand-carry up stairs
variations.when: Only when no mechanical delivery path exists
changes: Last resort, not the plan — if this is the plan, the labor number is wrong
Two-person carries; never the default delivery method

quality_checks.prompt: Board split per room or zone from takeoff — not one pile per floor
MR, abuse-resistant, rated, and shaftwall board separated and labeled on the top sheet
Stacks flat, off slab, level base, out of weather
GC confirmed allowable floor loading before heavy staging on suspended slabs
Count, damage notes, and photos documented before driver leaves

common_mistakes.title: One pile per floor
common_mistakes.wrong: All board dropped at the elevator or stair landing
common_mistakes.right: Split per room or zone from the takeoff
common_mistakes.why: Every extra carry is unpaid labor and damage risk

common_mistakes.title: Mixed specialty stacks
common_mistakes.wrong: MR, rated, and standard board in one pile
common_mistakes.right: Separate stacks with a marker on the top sheet
common_mistakes.why: Wrong board on a rated wall fails inspection or forces tear-out

common_mistakes.title: Long-term edge storage
common_mistakes.wrong: Board leaned on edge for days
common_mistakes.why: Edge storage bows sheets — bowed board fights the hanger all day

common_mistakes.title: Stairs as the delivery plan
common_mistakes.wrong: Schedule assumes hand-carry up multiple flights
common_mistakes.right: Boom truck, telehandler, or window stocking ordered in advance
common_mistakes.why: Labor number is wrong and injury risk is high

provenance.note: Manufacturer storage-and-handling guidance (keep board flat, dry, off the ground, supported) is consistent across USG, National Gypsum, and CertainTeed. Boom-truck and specialty delivery practice is standard supplier-side material handling. Floor-loading limits are project-specific.
